procedural_history.originating_court: Director of Enforcement (adjudication proceedings under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated August 10, 1961, of the Calcutta High Court in Civil Rule No. 1428 of 1958, which accepted a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution and quashed the adjudication proceedings.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent (original petitioner) filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the Calcutta High Court challenging the adjudication proceedings. The grounds for the challenge were: (i) Section 23(1)(a) and Section 23D of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act contravened Article 14 of the Constitution; (ii) the 1957 amendment to the Act did not apply to contraventions before it came into force; and (iii) Section 23(1)(a) of the Act was ultra vires Article 20(1) of the Constitution. The High Court upheld the objections and quashed the adjudication proceedings. The petitioner was allowed to raise the point that s. 23 ( 1 )(a) as well as s. 23D contravened art. 14 of the Constitution.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Director of Enforcement appealed to the Supreme Court by certificate granted by the High Court of Calcutta under Article 132(1) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court accepted the appeal and dismissed the petition under Article 226, reversing the High Court's decision.

directions: The petition under art. E 226 dismissed.
The appellant will have his costs here and in the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether sections 23(1)(a) and 23D of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act were ultra vires of Article 20(2) of the Constitution.

facts: The respondent challenged adjudication proceedings initiated against them under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act.
One of the principal grounds for the challenge was that sections 23(1)(a) and 23D of the Act were ultra vires of Article 20(2) of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether sections 23(1)(a) and 23D of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act contravened Article 14 of the Constitution.

facts: The respondent argued that sections 23(1)(a) and 23D of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act were unconstitutional because they violated Article 14.
law: The Supreme Court had previously decided this issue in the case of Shanti Prasad Jain v. Director of Enforcement.
application: In the Shanti Prasad Jain case, the Court held that sections 23(1) and 23D of the Act did not violate Article 14 of the Constitution.
Faced with this established precedent, the counsel for the respondent conceded that he could not press the point any further.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, relying on its prior ruling in Shanti Prasad Jain v. Director of Enforcement, which established that the challenged sections did not violate Article 14 of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether a person accused of an offence has a vested right to be tried by a particular court or a particular procedure under Article 20 of the Constitution.

law.law_text: Article 20 of the Constitution prohibits only conviction or sentencing under an ex post facto law, not the trial itself under a different procedure.
It is a well-recognized general principle that no person has a vested right in any particular course of procedure.

A person accused of an offence does not have a fundamental right to be tried by a particular court or procedure, unless the change in procedure results in discrimination or the violation of another fundamental right.

application.law_text: Article 20 of the Constitution prohibits only conviction or sentencing under an ex post facto law, not the trial itself under a different procedure.
application.application_text: The Court distinguished between the trial and the conviction/sentence. It clarified that while Article 20 protects against being punished by a law made after the offence was committed, it does not prevent the trial from being conducted under a new procedure that came into force after the offence.

application.law_text: It is a well-recognized general principle that no person has a vested right in any particular course of procedure.
application.application_text: The Court applied this general rule, stating there was no reason it should not prevail in this case. It found that changes in procedure are generally retrospective, and the accused did not have a protected substantive right to the old procedure.

application.law_text: A person accused of an offence does not have a fundamental right to be tried by a particular court or procedure, unless the change in procedure results in discrimination or the violation of another fundamental right.
application.application_text: The Court explicitly stated that there is no principle within Article 20 that makes the right to a specific course of procedure a vested or fundamental right. Therefore, changing the court or the procedural rules for a trial is permissible, provided it does not introduce unconstitutional discrimination or violate other fundamental rights.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that an accused person does not have a vested right to be tried by a particular court or procedure. The Court reasoned that Article 20 only prohibits conviction or sentence under an ex post facto law, not the trial itself. It affirmed the general legal principle that no one has a vested right in a course of procedure, and a change in trial procedure can be applied retrospectively unless it is discriminatory or violates another fundamental right.

issue.issue_text: Whether the proposed adjudication for an offence committed in 1954 was illegal and without jurisdiction.

facts: The alleged offence, recovery of foreign currency, occurred in 1954.
At that time, the law only permitted criminal proceedings before a court for such an offence.
In 1957, the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act was amended, introducing an alternative procedure of 'adjudication proceedings' by the Director of Enforcement.
In 1958, the Director of Enforcement initiated these new adjudication proceedings against the respondent for the 1954 offence.

The respondent challenged this, and the High Court agreed, ruling that the respondent had a 'vested right to be tried by an ordinary court' and that the new procedure could not be applied retrospectively.
law: Article 20 of the Constitution prohibits conviction or sentencing under an ex post facto law, but it does not prohibit a trial under a different procedure than what existed at the time of the offence.
An accused person does not have a fundamental right to be tried by a particular court or by a particular procedure.
A change in the forum or procedure for a trial is considered a procedural matter, not a substantive one.
New procedural laws are generally understood to be retrospective in their application unless stated otherwise.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the 1957 amendment, which introduced adjudication proceedings, was a change in procedure, not a change in substantive law.
The Court reasoned that since the trial itself is not prohibited by Article 20, using a procedure different from the one in place in 1954 is not unconstitutional.

The Court rejected the High Court's view that the respondent had a 'vested right' to a trial in a specific court. It noted that since no criminal proceedings had ever been started under the old law, no rights, such as the right to appeal under the Criminal Procedure Code, had been affected or had become vested.
Therefore, applying the new procedural law of adjudication to an offence committed before the law was changed was permissible.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the adjudication was illegal and without jurisdiction. It held that the change in law was merely procedural and could be applied retrospectively to the offence committed in 1954. The Court found that the respondent had no fundamental or vested right to be tried by the procedure that existed at the time of the offence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a person accused of an offence has a vested right to be tried by a particular court or a particular procedure under Article 20 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The accused did not have a vested right to be tried by an ordinary criminal court.
The amendment only changed the venue of the trial from a Magistrate to the Director of Enforcement and did not affect any vested right.
A person accused of an offence has no vested right to be tried by a particular court or procedure, as established in Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh v. The State of Vindhya Pradesh.
respondent_arguments: A substantive vested right to be tried by an ordinary court existed before the amendment.
Alterations in procedure should not be retrospective if there is a good reason against it, and the principles of Article 20 provide such a reason.
The amending Act did not indicate that the new procedure would be retrospective, and applying it retrospectively affects the right of appeal under the Criminal Procedure Code.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the proposed adjudication for an offence committed in 1954 was illegal and without jurisdiction.
appellant_arguments: The amendment was a change in procedure or venue of trial, not a substantive change, and therefore could be applied to an offence committed before the amendment was passed.
Since there is no vested right in a particular procedure, applying the new adjudication process to the 1954 offence was legal and within jurisdiction.
respondent_arguments: The offence was committed in 1954, before the 1957 amendment introduced adjudication proceedings.
The proposed adjudication was therefore illegal and entirely without jurisdiction.
The amending Act did not specify that the new procedure would be retrospective.

cases.principle: A person accused of the commission of an offence has no vested right to be tried by a particular court or a particular procedure except in so far as there is any constitutional objection by way of discrimination or the violation of any other fundamental right is involved.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A person accused of the commission of an offence has no vested right to be tried by a particular court or a particular procedure, except where there is a constitutional objection by way of discrimination or the violation of any other fundamental right. There is no principle under Article 20 of the Constitution that makes a right to any course of procedure a vested right.
obiter: Section 23(1) and Section 23D of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act do not violate Article 14 of the Constitution.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A person accused of committing an offence does not have a vested right to be tried by a particular court or under a particular procedure. A legislative amendment that only changes the venue or procedure of a trial, such as moving it from a Magistrate to the Director of Enforcement for adjudication, is not a substantive change and does not engage the protections of Article 20 of the Constitution. Therefore, such a procedural change can be applied to an offence that was committed before the amendment was enacted.
legal_tests_applied: The distinction between a substantive right and a procedural right, where a change in procedure is not considered a vested right.
The principle from Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh v. The State of Vindhya Pradesh, which establishes that an accused person has no vested right to be tried by a particular court or procedure.
The precedent from Shanti Prasad Jain v. Director of Enforcement, which settled that sections 23(1) and 23D of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act do not violate Article 14 of the Constitution.
